To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the AIDS dementia complex is associated with infection by human immunofluence virus type 1, that the distribution of infected cells is highly nonrandom, and that there are important clinical‐virological correlates.

HIV‐1 infection of the brain is not uniformly present and is limited to deep brain structures, and that the clinical severity of AIDS dementia complex is not directly related to the extent and distribution of brain infection.

HIV‐1 p 24 core protein was detected in macroglial and microglial cells, but not in neurons, in the brains of patients with AIDS, that the distribution of HIV‐1 p‐24 positive cells was preferentially associated with the basal ganglia and the white matter and was not uniformly distributed throughout the brain, and that the presence of HIV‐1 infection in the brain correlated with the severity of clinical AIDS dementia complex (stage of dementia).
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new model for the pathogenesis of AIDS dementia.
the relationship of HIV‐1 brain infections and AIDS dementia complex (AIDS dementia).
the development of a new approach to the study of the development of AIDS dementia complex (ADCD).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV‐1 infection of the brain is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for the clinical syndrome of ADC, and that the severity of ADC is related to the extent of brain infection.
the presence of HIV‐1 antigen in the brains of patients with ADC correlates with the severity of clinical dysfunction but that this correlation is far from absolute.
AIDS‐dementia is not caused by the HIV‐1 virus, although it can certainly be caused by other factors that may or may not be related to the virus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of HIV‐1 antigen in the brain of patients with ADC is highly correlated with the presence of ADC, but the presence of ADC is not highly correlated with the extent of HIV‐1 brain antigen.
HIV‐1 infection of the central nervous system is not a necessary or sufficient cause of AIDS dementia.

the HIV‐1 brain disease in AIDS patients is characterized by a selective and limited infection of deep brain structures, and that the clinical severity of AIDS‐related neurological dysfunction is related to the extent and location of brain infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the presence and frequency with which HIV‐1 p 24 antigen is detected in the brains of AIDS patients is correlated with clinical severity, suggesting that the virus is a major pathogenetic factor in the development of AIDS dementia.
there is a correlation between HIV‐1 infection and the clinical severity of the disease.
HIV‐1 is a neurotropic pathogen, and that the CNS is a target for HIV‐1 infection.
